title: Given the head of a singly linked list, determine whether it reads the same forward and backward. Aim for linear time and constant extra space. (LeetCode: Palindrome Linked List)
shortTitle: Palindrome LinkedList (Find Middle, Reverse Half, Compare)

s1_definition.profdef: Checking whether a linked list is a palindrome in constant space combines three techniques: use fast-slow pointers to find the middle, reverse the second half of the list in place, then compare the first half with the reversed second half node by node. Optionally the second half is reversed again to restore the original list. This runs in linear time with constant extra space.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine Rajesh has a chain of linked digits forming a reference code and wants to know if it is a mirror image of itself, the same read from either end. He finds the middle of the chain with the fast-slow walker trick, flips the second half around so it points backward, and then walks the first half and the flipped second half together comparing digit by digit. If every pair matches, the code is a palindrome. To be polite he can flip the second half back to leave the chain as he found it.
s1_definition.oneliner: Find the middle, reverse the second half, compare the two halves, then optionally reverse back.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Checking whether a linked list is a palindrome in constant space combines three techniques: use fast-slow pointers to find the middle, reverse the second half of the list in place, then compare the first half with the reversed second half node by node. Optionally the second half is reversed again to restore the original list. This runs in linear time with constant extra space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine Rajesh has a chain of linked digits forming a reference code and wants to know if it is a mirror image of itself, the same read from either end. He finds the middle of the chain with the fast-slow walker trick, flips the second half around so it points backward, and then walks the first half and the flipped second half together comparing digit by digit. If every pair matches, the code is a palindrome. To be polite he can flip the second half back to leave the chain as he found it.

**One line to remember:** Find the middle, reverse the second half, compare the two halves, then optionally reverse back.

sections.s2_technical:
The easy approach copies all the values into an array or list and then checks the array with two indices from both ends, which is clear but uses extra space proportional to the length. The constant-space approach manipulates the list itself.

First we find the middle using the fast-slow pointer technique: slow moves one node, fast moves two, and when fast reaches the end, slow is at the midpoint. Second, we reverse the portion of the list from the midpoint onward using the standard in-place reversal with a previous, current, and next pointer, which flips each node's next pointer to point backward. Third, we walk one pointer from the head and another from the new head of the reversed second half, comparing their values; if any pair differs, the list is not a palindrome. Finally, as a courtesy and to avoid leaving the data structure corrupted, we reverse the second half again to restore the original order.

A finance usage example: suppose a code chain is `1 -> 2 -> 2 -> 1`. The middle is found, the second half `2 -> 1` is reversed to `1 -> 2`, and then we compare: first half starts at 1 and reversed half starts at 1, they match; next 2 and 2 match. All pairs match, so the code is a palindrome.

The senior-level nuance: reversing the second half mutates the list, so in a shared or concurrent context we must either restore it afterward or document that the method is destructive, and restoring it keeps the method side-effect free from the caller's perspective. Handling odd length is natural because the single middle node does not need a partner in the comparison. The comparison loop should stop when the reversed-half pointer becomes null, since the reversed half is never longer than the first half. The array-copy method is simpler and perfectly acceptable unless constant space is explicitly required.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India uses certain symmetric reference codes for a verification feature, where a valid code must read the same forward and backward, stored as a linked chain of digits. The verifier must confirm the symmetry efficiently, and because the chains can be long and the service is memory sensitive, copying all the digits into a separate structure is discouraged.

Problem 2 — The original chain is used immediately afterward by another step, so the verifier must leave the chain in its original order after checking, meaning any in-place reversal must be undone before returning.

The code defines a `PalindromeCodeChecker` class with an `isPalindrome` method that finds the middle, reverses the second half, compares, and then restores the list. A runnable demo checks a palindrome code and a non-palindrome code and logs the results.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: the palindrome chain `1 -> 2 -> 2 -> 1` and the non-palindrome chain `1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4`.

Step 1: For `1 -> 2 -> 2 -> 1`, the fast-slow walk finds the middle. Slow lands on the second 2, the start of the second half.

Step 2: The method reverses the second half starting at that node, turning `2 -> 1` into `1 -> 2`. The second head now points to the node holding 1.

Step 3: Comparison begins. The first-half pointer starts at the head holding 1 and the reversed-half pointer starts at the node holding 1; they match. Both advance, comparing 2 against 2; they match. The reversed-half pointer becomes null, ending the comparison with all pairs equal, so the chain is a palindrome.

Step 4: The method reverses the second half again to restore the original `1 -> 2 -> 2 -> 1`, leaving the chain untouched for the next step.

Step 5: For `1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4`, the second half `3 -> 4` reverses to `4 -> 3`. The comparison pits the head 1 against 4, which differ immediately, so the method reports not a palindrome and then restores the chain.

Final output:

```
Oct 27, 2026 7:10:00 PM com.bank.verify.PalindromeDemo main
INFO: Code chain is a palindrome (valid).
INFO: 1221 palindrome: true
WARNING: Code chain is NOT a palindrome.
INFO: 1234 palindrome: false
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Chain 1→2→2→1
    │ fast-slow → middle at 2nd '2'
    │ reverse 2nd half: 2→1 becomes 1→2
    ▼
  compare: head 1 vs 1, 2 vs 2 → palindrome
    │ reverse back → 1→2→2→1 restored
    ▼
  result: true

  Chain 1→2→3→4
    reverse 2nd half 3→4 → 4→3
    compare head 1 vs 4 → not palindrome → restore
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Checking whether a linked list is a palindrome in constant extra space is a beautiful composition of three fundamental techniques. The naive approach copies all the values into an array and checks it with two indices from both ends, which is clear but uses linear extra space; the constant-space approach manipulates the list itself.

First I find the middle of the list with the fast-slow pointer technique, where the slow pointer moves one node and the fast pointer moves two, so the slow pointer lands on the midpoint when the fast pointer reaches the end. Second I reverse the second half of the list in place using the standard previous-current-next reversal, flipping each node's pointer to face backward. Third I walk one pointer from the head and another from the new head of the reversed second half, comparing values node by node, and if any pair differs the list is not a palindrome. Finally I reverse the second half again to restore the list to its original order, so the method leaves no side effects behind.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this in a verification feature that relied on symmetric reference codes stored as linked chains of digits, where a valid code had to read the same forward and backward. The chains could be long and the service was memory sensitive, so copying all the digits into a separate structure was discouraged, and the in-place approach met the constant-space requirement. Critically, the original chain was used by the very next step in the flow, so restoring it after the check was not optional.

The senior-level point I emphasize is the restoration and the correctness details. Because reversing the second half mutates the list, in any shared or concurrent context I either restore it afterward or clearly document that the method is destructive, and restoring it is what makes the method safe for the caller. Odd-length lists are handled naturally, because the single middle node has no partner to compare against, and I stop the comparison when the reversed-half pointer becomes null since that half is never longer than the first. Being able to explain both the composition of the three techniques and the obligation to leave the data structure as I found it is what demonstrates production-level thinking rather than a textbook answer.
